review: The Model Y remains the default EV crossover for a reason: it does everything competently and a few things brilliantly. The 2025 Long Range trim's 357-mile EPA rating is best-in-class for a mainstream crossover, and the Supercharger network still makes it the easiest EV in America to road-trip — plan on roughly 27 minutes for a 10-80% top-up at up to 250 kW. Acceleration (5.4 seconds to 60) is more than adequate, though the ride leans firm over broken pavement, a Tesla hallmark that hasn't fully softened even after the Juniper refresh. Cargo capacity of 76.2 cubic feet with the rear seats folded beats nearly every rival in this class, frunk included. At $46,630 to start, it isn't cheap, but nothing else combines charging infrastructure, range, and interior volume this well. The minimalist cabin and touchscreen-everything control scheme will still frustrate traditionalists, but as an ownership proposition, the Model Y is hard to beat.

Tesla's sedan remains the sharper-driving sibling to the Model Y, and the numbers back it up: the Long Range RWD's 363-mile EPA rating is among the best of any EV sold in America, and 0-60 in 4.2 seconds feels genuinely quick without tipping into Performance-trim harshness. The chassis rewards a spirited backroad pass in a way few electric sedans manage, though the tradeoff is a stiffer ride that transmits more road texture than the Model Y. Supercharger access again does the heavy lifting on road trips — 250 kW peak, roughly 27 minutes for a 10-80% fill. Where it disappoints is cargo: 23 cubic feet of trunk-plus-frunk space is tight for anyone hauling more than luggage and a stroller. Starting around $43,000 for Long Range, it undercuts most rivals with comparable range. For buyers who prioritize efficiency and driving feel over outright interior volume, it's still the class benchmark.

GM finally built an EV that feels like a genuine value play rather than a compliance vehicle. At $34,995, the Equinox EV undercuts nearly every electric crossover on this list while delivering a 319-mile range on its better trims, a quiet, well-isolated cabin, and interior space reviewers keep comparing to a small living room. The catch is charging: real-world testing has clocked peak DC rates around 60 kW even on 100-kW-plus chargers, turning a 15-90% top-up into an 80-minute affair — noticeably slower than Hyundai's or Tesla's fast-charging speed. Performance is similarly modest; the base front-driver is fine around town but runs out of breath at highway speed. Cold weather takes a real bite out of the advertised 319 miles, too. Still, with 57.2 cubic feet of total cargo space and genuinely upscale fit and finish for the price, the Equinox EV earns its reputation as the segment's value leader — just don't buy it expecting a road-trip charging champion.

Ford dressed up an electric crossover in pony-car branding, and the driving experience mostly lives up to it — the GT trim's acceleration and eager turn-in give it more personality than most electric SUVs manage. Base Select trims are more modest, with a 6.5-second 0-60 and a 260-mile range that extended-battery models push closer to 320. The ride gets busy over broken pavement, and front-seat adjustability is more limited than rivals offer. Charging is the Mach-E's clearest weak spot: independent testing has repeatedly flagged it as one of the slower DC fast-charging EVs in its class, undercutting the road-trip case even when range numbers check out. Cargo space (34.4 cubic feet, 60 with seats folded) splits the difference between the tighter Ioniq 5 and the roomier Model Y. Starting at $37,995, it's a reasonably priced, genuinely fun-to-drive EV crossover held back mainly by charging speed and ride refinement.

The Ioniq 5 pairs genuinely striking design with the kind of charging performance that makes road trips painless — its 800-volt architecture supports up to 350 kW, adding meaningful range in about 18 minutes and leaving the Mach-E and ID.4 well behind. Ride quality is a highlight too: the suspension soaks up rough pavement with a composure that belies the car's crossover proportions, and cabin noise is impressively well controlled. Acceleration on dual-motor versions is genuinely rapid, with real-world range testing routinely beating the EPA sticker. The compromise is cargo space — at 27.2 cubic feet with a nearly useless front trunk, it's noticeably tighter than the Model Y or Blazer EV. Starting at $42,600 for the Standard Range trim, value is strong across the lineup, especially once you factor in Hyundai's generous warranty. For buyers who charge on the road more than at home, the Ioniq 5 is arguably the smartest pick here.

Built on GM's Ultium platform, the Prologue is Honda's admission that building an EV platform from scratch wasn't worth the effort — and it shows in a driving experience that feels borrowed rather than distinctly Honda. Acceleration is middling (6.2 seconds to 60 on the range-topping AWD trim) and handling doesn't distinguish itself from the Blazer EV it's mechanically related to. Real-world range is a genuine strength, though: Honda's 308-mile FWD rating has been beaten in independent testing, with 320 miles achieved in real conditions. Charging, unfortunately, lags noticeably behind class leaders like the Ioniq 5, roughly doubling the time needed for an equivalent range top-up. Cargo space, at 23.7 cubic feet and no frunk, trails most rivals too. Starting near $47,400, it's priced like a distinctive vehicle without quite delivering distinctive engineering — competent and quiet, but not a compelling reason beyond the badge.

The Lightning proved an electric F-150 could still feel like an F-150 — composed, spacious, and quick, with instant torque that makes it startlingly fast off the line for a vehicle this size. Extended Range models manage up to 320 miles EPA, though owners should expect a real-world hit of 20-35% in cold weather and worse at sustained highway speeds, especially while towing (rated up to 10,000 lbs with the Max Trailer Tow package). DC fast charging takes roughly 41 minutes for a 15-80% fill, workable but not class-leading. The 14.1-cubic-foot lockable frunk adds genuine utility on top of standard bed capacity. Pricing has crept up since the Lightning's 2022 debut — well-equipped trims now push into the mid-$60,000s. For buyers who charge at home and stay under roughly 150 miles a day, it's an excellent daily truck; for heavy towing or road-trip duty, the range math gets considerably less flattering.

No vehicle on this list generates more strong opinions, and the driving experience mostly justifies the attention: acceleration is genuinely startling, and the stainless-steel panels and 123-kWh battery give it real road presence. The Long Range trim's 335-mile EPA rating and 250-kW peak charging are respectable for a vehicle this size and heavy. But the Cybertruck's angular shape works against everyday usability — the bed is harder to load than a conventional truck's, the frunk is smaller than rivals', and the letterbox rear window makes visibility genuinely poor. The cabin, while roomy up front, doesn't feel especially premium for a vehicle starting near $72,000 and climbing past $100,000 for the Cyberbeast. Interior noise — creaks, gear whine, tire roar — is more noticeable than in other Teslas. It's an undeniable spectacle and legitimately quick, but as a practical work truck or family hauler, several rivals here do the job with far fewer compromises.

The R1S delivers the most convincing case yet that a three-row electric SUV can also be genuinely fast — the tri-motor variant hits 60 mph in under 3 seconds, an absurd number for a 7-seat family vehicle. Range is strong across the lineup, with real-world testing landing close to or above EPA figures on the 371- and 410-mile trims. The first two rows are comfortable and nicely finished, though the third row is tight enough that it's best reserved for kids or short trips. Charging speed is the R1S's most notable shortfall — middling compared to the fastest-charging rivals here, despite Rivian's growing Adventure Network. Cargo practicality is a genuine strength: a large frunk plus 32.6 cubic feet behind the third row (90.7 with seats folded) make it one of the most usable SUVs on this list. Starting at $75,900, it's expensive, but direct sales and generous standard equipment make the value case better than the sticker price suggests.

The Blazer EV is the more style-focused, more powerful sibling to the Equinox EV, and it drives like it — smooth around town, composed at highway speeds, and quick enough (roughly 6 seconds to 60 in AWD trim) to feel genuinely sporty without needing the range-topping SS. Its 85-102 kWh battery options stretch EPA range from 283 to 334 miles depending on trim, and the one-pedal driving mode is well tuned for daily use. Charging is its weak point: DC fast-charge speeds trail class leaders like the Ioniq 5 by a wide margin, roughly doubling the time needed for an equivalent range top-up. At $46,095 to start, it's priced higher than the closely related Equinox EV without a proportional jump in capability, though steep real-world discounts have made it more competitive than the sticker suggests. With 59.1 cubic feet of total cargo space, it's spacious and genuinely pleasant to drive — just don't expect Ioniq-level charging convenience.

The ID.4 remains a solid, unglamorous choice — comfortable, reasonably practical, and priced to compete, but never quite exciting. The entry Standard trim's 62-kWh battery delivers a modest 206-mile EPA range, while independent testing has shown it can exceed 299 miles in mixed-condition driving on higher trims, suggesting Volkswagen's estimates run conservative. Front-seat comfort and highway ride quality earn consistent praise, though bigger bumps produce noticeable body motion, and the interior materials feel a step below the segment's best. Handling is competent but uninspired — nobody cross-shopping a Mustang Mach-E for driving thrills will pick the ID.4 instead. DC fast charging is only slightly below average for the class, with roughly 17 minutes needed to add 100 miles on the larger battery. At $39,995 to start, it's a sensible, well-built entry point into EV ownership, especially now that VW has trimmed pricing to stay competitive.

Cadillac's electric flagship is the most convincing argument yet that American luxury EVs can compete with German rivals on substance, not just price. The RWD's 326-mile EPA range and 102-kWh battery are genuinely competitive, and the cabin — anchored by a 33-inch curved display — delivers a plush, tech-forward experience that undercuts equivalent Audi and BMW electric SUVs by a meaningful margin. Super Cruise, GM's hands-free driving system, works across more than 400,000 miles of North American highway and remains one of the most polished driver-assist systems available at any price. Acceleration is adequate in RWD form and genuinely brisk in the 515-horsepower AWD variant. DC fast charging adds roughly 85 miles in 10 minutes — solid, if not segment-leading. Starting near $58,590, the Lyriq undercuts its German competition while matching or beating their interior ambiance.

BMW's smallest EV sedan splits the difference between engineering rigor and brand tax. The eDrive40's 318-mile EPA figure is competitive, and 200kW DC charging gets you from 10-80% in roughly half an hour — solid, not spectacular. What sells the i4 is the chassis: rear-drive balance, a suspension that irons out broken pavement, and a cabin quiet enough to make the motor's whisper feel like a feature. 5.3 seconds to 60 mph is brisk without threatening the M50's actual quickness. The real friction point is money — at $57,900 to start, and climbing fast once you add options, the i4 asks a real premium over a Model 3 or Ioniq 6 for similar range and less rear headroom. Cargo is where the hatchback design earns its keep: 10 cubic feet up front, nearly 17 with seats folded. A genuinely good sports sedan wearing an EV drivetrain — just don't expect a bargain.

Audi's new PPE platform pays off immediately in ride quality — the standard air suspension delivers a hushed, controlled float that few electric SUVs at any price manage. The Q6 e-tron's 800-volt architecture pushes DC charging to 270kW, meaning a 10-80% top-up in about 21 minutes, among the quickest of any crossover on this list. Range tops out near 321 miles on the rear-drive trim, 298 on quattro — both class-competitive, and owners report hitting those numbers in real driving. Acceleration (4.9 seconds to 60) is confident rather than thrilling, which suits the car's grand-touring character. Cabin materials occasionally undercut the $63,800 starting price, and the regen-braking logic can feel fussy when you brake normally. Cargo is respectable at 30.2 cubic feet, 60.2 with seats down. Polished, quick-charging, and genuinely pleasant to live with — it just costs Audi money to remind you it's a luxury product.

The EV9 does the unglamorous work of a three-row SUV extremely well. Kia's 800V platform charges 10-80% in about 24 minutes, and independent testing has beaten the EPA number outright — 306 miles recorded against a 304-mile rating on the GT-Line Long Range, which almost never happens. Cargo maxes out at 81.7 cubic feet with the third row folded, and 5,000 pounds of tow capacity makes it a legitimate family hauler, not just an EV with extra seats. The base Light RWD trim is underpowered, but Wind and GT-Line models near 4.7 seconds to 60 feel appropriately quick for something this size. Seats are genuinely plush up front — heated, ventilated, some with massage — though the third row is tighter than the rest. At $54,900 to start, this is the rare three-row EV that doesn't punish you for wanting one; it undercuts most of the segment while out-charging and out-hauling it.

The Hummer EV is a spectacle first, a vehicle second. 1,000 horsepower and a claimed 3.0-second 0-60 in a truck weighing 8,660 pounds is a genuine party trick, and the four-wheel-steering CrabWalk theatrics make an absurd amount of mass feel maneuverable. That mass is the problem everywhere else. GM's roughly 200kWh pack returns only around 1.6 miles per kWh, among the worst efficiency figures of any EV sold, and DC charging that peaks near 300kW in ideal conditions drops to a real-world average closer to 180-240kW — expect 45 minutes or more for a meaningful top-up. Ride quality is comfortable on the highway, softer and busier elsewhere. Starting around $96,550 and climbing past $107,000 for the pickup's EV3X, the Hummer asks a lot for something GM itself effectively admits you can get most of the goodness of in a cheaper Cadillac. Spectacle has a price, and here it's steep.

Toyota came to the EV fight late, and the bZ4X still shows it. Edmunds' real-world test returned just 227 miles against a 252-mile EPA rating for the FWD model — one of the larger range shortfalls tested, and reason enough to shop carefully if you road-trip. Charging tops out at a modest 150kW on FWD trims and a genuinely slow 100kW on AWD, both trailing the segment by a wide margin. The upside is price: $37,070 to start undercuts most competitors substantially, and the ride is composed if unremarkable, with supportive if unexciting front seats. Acceleration is adequate for commuting duty but nothing more. Storage disappoints throughout — no frunk, an undersized console, a missing glovebox — and there's no towing capability at all. It's affordable and it works, but almost everything else on this list does more for similar or less money.

The Ariya's strongest case is refinement: a quiet, well-cushioned cabin that rides smoothly over broken pavement and feels genuinely upscale for $39,770. That's largely where the praise ends. DC fast-charging peaks at just 130kW, translating to roughly 40 minutes for a 20-80% charge — noticeably behind rivals with 800V architecture, and home charging via 240V stretches past 10 hours. The base 63kWh battery's 216-mile EPA range is modest by 2025 standards, and efficiency testing shows the Ariya using more energy per mile than most competitors. Handling is soft, with noticeable body lean in corners, and even the quicker dual-motor version's 5.3-second run to 60 won't excite anyone. Storage for small items is tight, and towing capacity caps at a token 1,500 pounds. Comfortable and quiet, but thoroughly outpaced on the numbers that matter now.

The EV6 remains one of the best-engineered EVs at its price, and the charging numbers prove it: Kia's 800-volt architecture gets a 10-80% top-up in around 18 minutes, second in this group only to the Ioniq 5's shared platform. Testers have beaten the EPA estimate outright — 296 miles recorded against a 237-mile rating on one trim — suggesting Kia under-promises here. The GT-Line's 4.9-second sprint to 60 feels genuinely brisk, and one-pedal driving is tuned well for daily use, even if the chassis isn't especially playful on a curvy road. Seats are supportive with excellent rear legroom, though the coupe-like roofline eats into headroom. At $42,900 to start, it costs a bit more than some crossover rivals, but build quality and a long warranty justify it. The real weakness is cargo — 24.4 cubic feet trails traditional SUV rivals like the Model Y by a wide margin. Quick, efficient, slightly cramped in back.

Cadillac's smallest EV nails efficiency and undercuts its own numbers in the right direction — testers logged 339 miles against a 302-mile EPA rating, a rare and welcome overachievement. The 85kWh pack and 300-horsepower dual-motor setup deliver a middling 5.9-second 0-60, and body lean in corners confirms this isn't the sporty Cadillac the badge sometimes promises. Where the Optiq clearly disappoints is charging: 150kW peak DC input lags well behind rivals at this price, turning road-trip stops into a genuine inconvenience. The cabin, though, punches above its $52,895 starting price — upscale materials, generous standard tech, and 26 cubic feet of cargo (57 with seats folded) that beats similarly sized rivals. Front seats are well-padded and comfortable; rear seats are tighter for taller passengers. Bluetooth-only phone integration, with no CarPlay or Android Auto, is a genuinely odd omission at this level. A composed, efficient, slow-charging value play.

Built on GM's Ultium platform, the ZDX trades in hushed, substantial luxury-SUV comfort rather than outright excitement — quiet at speed, low to the ground for easy entry, with instant torque that makes everyday acceleration feel effortless even in the base A-Spec RWD's 5.5-second run to 60. The Type S sharpens that to 4.3 seconds if you want it. Real-world range is where the ZDX gets honest fast: the 313-mile EPA rating for A-Spec RWD is achievable in mild weather, but cold-climate owners report meaningfully lower results, with practical everyday range closer to 200 miles. DC charging peaks around 190kW, good for a 30-40 minute 10-80% session — competent, not class-leading. Handling turns noticeably soft, almost sloshy, if you push it in corners, and rear headroom is tight for taller passengers. At roughly $64,500 to start, it undercuts the Cadillac Lyriq while matching most of its comfort.

Chevy built the Silverado EV to answer a specific question — can an electric truck actually work — and mostly it does. Independent testing returned 484 miles on the Extended Range pack, beating its own EPA estimate and putting real distance between it and every other EV pickup on sale. The 350kW peak charging rate is genuinely quick, and 4.4 seconds to 60 is brisk, if on the slower side for the segment's power ceiling. The eTrunk frunk plus a midgate that opens the bed to nearly nine feet of load length make this a legitimately useful work truck, backed by a 12,500-pound tow rating. What holds it back is money and finish: starting around $73,100 and climbing well past $90,000 on higher trims, with interior plastics that feel cheap for the price and more road noise than expected at highway speeds. Chevy solved the hard engineering problem here; it hasn't yet solved the value one.

Lucid's engineering advantage is obvious within the first mile. The Air Pure's 420-mile EPA range and roughly 27 kWh/100-mile efficiency come from genuinely superior packaging, not just a bigger battery, and the ride — composed, precise, best-in-class territory — backs up the drivetrain numbers. 4.5 seconds to 60 feels quicker than the spec suggests thanks to sharp, well-weighted steering that never turns twitchy. Charging is good, not great: roughly 17 minutes for 200 miles added, competent but not the fastest in this group. Cargo is a genuine strength for a sedan — 32.1 cubic feet split between a 22.1-cubic-foot trunk and 10-cubic-foot frunk, more useful than most crossovers here. At $69,900 to start, the Pure undercuts comparable German luxury sedans meaningfully while beating most of them on range and efficiency, even if some interior trim pieces and panel gaps betray Lucid's smaller-scale manufacturing. The shrewd buy for anyone cross-shopping a Mercedes EQS or BMW i7.

The iX is proof BMW can still build a genuinely great electric vehicle when it isn't worried about matching a combustion sibling's shape. The 309-mile EPA rating undersells it badly — independent testing hit 377 miles on a single charge, one of the largest positive gaps on this list. Acceleration is serious in both directions: 4.2 seconds to 60 in xDrive50 form, 3.5 in the M60, each backed by steering that stays composed even when pushed. Charging is among the quickest of any luxury SUV here, and BMW throws in two years of complimentary Electrify America charging to sweeten the deal. Cabin quality is the highlight — quilted seats, a low floor for easy entry, generous rear space with its own climate zones — while 35.5 cubic feet of cargo beats rivals like the Cadillac Lyriq outright. The $87,250 starting price escalates quickly with options, and the styling remains genuinely divisive, but the engineering underneath is close to the class benchmark.

The Model X remains Tesla's weirdest flex: falcon-wing doors that still turn heads (and occasionally clip low garages), wrapped around a three-row SUV that's shockingly quick for something this size. Base all-wheel-drive models hit 60 mph in 3.8 seconds; step up to Plaid and it's a genuine hypercar-slayer at 2.5, absurd for a family hauler. The 335-mile range and 250-kW Supercharging access make it one of the easiest long-haul EVs to live with — replenish 10-80% in about half an hour, faster if you catch a V4 stall. Where it stumbles is everyday usability: the third row is a squeeze for adults, the glass roof cooks occupants without the optional shade, and there's still no CarPlay. At north of $85K as tested, it's asking premium money for an interior that feels more Silicon Valley minimalist than Bentley plush. Still, nothing else moves seven people, tows 5,000 pounds, and sprints like a sports car quite this effortlessly.
